claim_1.disposition: The durable, sourceable statement is that the reference implementation's shipped pattern for this device class is multi-app autologon. Azure/WindowsAppKiosk's solution-specific documentation (source/WindowsApp/README.md, pinned SHA 17e1c09b4883ea2062bef801ae24bbc9722861d7) enumerates exactly two deployment modes for the Windows App kiosk solution -- Multi-App Kiosk Mode and Shell Launcher Mode -- and the AssignedAccess/ folder at the same pinned SHA contains exactly two subfolders matching those modes, MultiApp/ and ShellLauncher/. RCP-06(a) and RCP-07(a) may state this positive claim as fact. No claim is made in either direction about what a third mode named only in the repository's root-level marketing bullet would or would not count as shipping -- that question is genuinely ambiguous in the upstream source and is not resolved here, per D-43.

claim_2.claim_as_stated: Whether the AssignedAccess CSP ShellLauncher node's licensing gate (the 'Class is not licensed for use' failure, Intune error -2016281112) is activation-based, as distinct from edition-based -- the mechanism RE-237:31, RCP-07(c) and RCP-08 currently state as fact.
claim_2.fetch_instrument: Playwright headless-browser navigation plus in-page JavaScript evaluation (`page.evaluate` reading `document.querySelector('main').innerText` and document `<meta>` tags) against the live, fully-rendered Microsoft Learn page. Chosen deliberately over WebFetch: WebFetch performs LLM summarization of fetched content, which is the specific failure mode this project has already recorded (`reference_canonical_source_bytes_not_webfetch.md` -- the same URL returned contradictory answers to two agents in one session). Reading the rendered DOM's own text nodes and meta tags is the actual source bytes the page serves to a browser, not a third party's summary of them. A bare `curl` was tried first and rejected -- it returns only ~350 words of pre-render skeleton HTML against this page's much larger rendered content, confirming 155-RESEARCH.md's own Pitfall 1 finding this session. Microsoft Learn's own full-text search (learn.microsoft.com/search) was used for the targeted troubleshooting-article search. GitHub's issues REST API was used for the corroborating source.

queries_run: "Class is not licensed for use" on learn.microsoft.com/search
targeted_search.finding: No first-party Microsoft troubleshooting article specifically about the AssignedAccess ShellLauncher CSP node and this error code or error string was located by either query. The error code itself is documented (by a Microsoft Q&A community response, not a first-party KB) as a generic, non-specific Intune remediation-failure code reused across unrelated policy classes -- password policy, WiFi profiles, BitLocker, Application Guard -- none of which are AssignedAccess/ShellLauncher. This is the specific gap 155-RESEARCH.md's Assumptions Log A3 flagged as not yet closed; it remains open after this session's targeted search.

corroborating_source.title: Shell Launcher V2 is not working on Windows 11 Pro 22H2
corroborating_source.symptom_reported: Identical error string, 'Class is not licensed for use', reported as an AssignedAccess operational event when enabling ShellLauncher via WMI.
corroborating_source.root_cause: The reporting device is explicitly Windows 11 Pro (stated in the issue title and body). Per the verbatim_sentence fetched above, the ShellLauncher node's edition-scope table lists Pro as unsupported (the CSP page's own edition table shows Enterprise/Education/IoT Enterprise supported, Pro explicitly excluded) -- this is an EDITION failure, matching the first-party edition-only gate exactly. It is not an activation failure: nothing in the issue names activation status, and nothing in the fetched first-party page conditions the gate on activation.

claim_2.disposition: UNVERIFIED for the activation mechanism, matching the predicted outcome. No first-party sentence fetched this session -- on the AssignedAccess CSP reference page itself, nor via two targeted searches for a troubleshooting article naming the specific Intune error code or error string -- states or implies that the ShellLauncher node's licensing gate depends on activation status as distinct from edition. The only first-party statement of the gate is edition-only: 'Shell Launcher as a feature and the ShellLauncher node both require Windows Enterprise or Windows Education to function. The ShellLauncher node is not supported in Windows 10 Pro.' The corroborating GitHub issue's root cause (Windows 11 Pro, an edition failure) matches this edition-only gate and does not corroborate an activation-based mechanism. Per this outcome, the mechanism claim is removed from documents that currently state it as fact (RE-237:31, out of this plan's file scope -- see plan 155-05; RE-224:29 RCP-07(c); licensing-matrix.md RCP-08, both in this plan). The raw pilot observation -- the 'Class is not licensed for use' error firing on an installed-but-reportedly-unactivated Enterprise image during the pilot -- is retained, labelled as a pilot observation, not as documented Microsoft mechanism. NO HALT: this outcome matches the predicted unverified resolution RESEARCH.md and CONTEXT.md D-44 anticipated, so Tasks 2 and 3 proceed on this disposition.

rcp_08_remedy_clause.claim_as_stated: RCP-08's remedy clause -- that a per-device volume key or purpose-built hardware IS REQUIRED to resolve the licensing gap a self-deploying kiosk hits.
rcp_08_remedy_clause.fetch_instrument: Direct read of this repository's own already-authored content (not an external fetch) -- this claim is outside RCP-10's two-external-claim scope per D-45, so it is resolved against what the pilot actually tested versus what is reasoned from documented licensing structure, not against a new external source.

sources.purpose: Confirm the pilot-authored reasoning already in RE-237 Step 4 about per-user vs. per-device activation paths (KMS/AD-BA/MAK), which is the basis for the reasoned-consequence wording -- not evidence that a volume key was tested.
sources.result: Verbatim: "Per-user Windows Enterprise E3/E5 cannot license a device nobody signs into. Volume licensing offers three activation methods: KMS needs a routed path to the KMS host and expires in 180 days without it; Active Directory-Based Activation needs a domain-joined device; MAK activates once over the internet and is the only one that fits an Entra-only, internet-only kiosk." This is reasoning about which volume-licensing method would fit the constraints, not a report that any of the three, or a volume key, was actually applied and tested in the pilot.

sources.purpose: Confirm the incumbent Windows Subscription Activation row and its two blockquotes are the site RCP-08's consequence and remedy language land in, and that neither currently mentions a volume key.
sources.result: Row: '| Windows Subscription Activation (Pro->Enterprise) | Microsoft 365 E3, E5, or A3/A5 | NOT available in Business Premium or F-series; manual OS upgrade required without this |'. Neither the row nor its two blockquotes mention a volume key, MAK, or purpose-built hardware today.

rcp_08_remedy_clause.disposition: The remedy clause is neither first-party-sourced nor pilot-observed -- the pilot never tested a volume key, a MAK activation, or purpose-built (already-activated) hardware; it only hit the failure and stopped at the multi-app branch that does not require activation. It must NOT be labelled as a pilot observation ([PILOT]), because that would assert an event that never happened. It must also not ship as unqualified fact. It will instead be worded as the reasoned consequence of the licensing structure already documented in this repository's own RE-237 Step 4 content: a per-user entitlement cannot license a device nobody signs into, so a self-deploying kiosk needs a device-scoped activation path instead (of which a per-device volume key is the one already-documented candidate that fits an Entra-only, internet-only device) -- attributed explicitly to reasoning from the licensing structure, not to a test that was run.
